title: Two Victories and a Costly Release
overview: Israel's king Ahab beats a much larger Aramean army twice with the LORD's help, then lets the enemy king go free and is condemned by a prophet for it.

parts.label: Ben-Hadad's demands (vv. 1-12)
parts.note: The king of Aram, a kingdom to the north centred on Damascus, besieges Israel's capital and demands Ahab's wealth and family, then raises the demand to looting every house. Ahab gives in at first, but his elders tell him to refuse, and he answers with a proverb: don't boast of victory before the battle is fought.

parts.label: Victory at Samaria (vv. 13-21)
parts.note: A prophet promises that a small band of young officers will defeat the huge army, so Ahab will know the LORD is God. They attack at noon while Ben-Hadad and his allied kings are drunk, and the Arameans scatter.

parts.label: God of the hills? (vv. 22-30)
parts.note: Ben-Hadad's advisers decide Israel won because its god only had power in hill country, so they plan the next spring's battle on flat ground with a rebuilt army. The LORD answers that mistake by giving Israel another victory, though the very large casualty numbers may be exaggerated or use 'thousand' for military units, and scholars are unsure which.

parts.label: Ahab spares Ben-Hadad (vv. 31-34)
parts.note: Sackcloth, rough cloth worn in grief, and ropes on the head were signs of total surrender, and Ahab responds by calling Ben-Hadad 'my brother' and seating him in his chariot. In return Ahab gets back lost cities and trading rights in Damascus, and he lets the enemy king go under a treaty.

parts.label: A prophet's staged story (vv. 35-43)
parts.note: A prophet has himself wounded and disguised, then tells Ahab a made-up story about letting a prisoner escape, and Ahab unknowingly condemns himself. The prophet says Ben-Hadad had been marked for death by the LORD, so Ahab and his people will pay instead; the harsh fate of the man who refused to strike the prophet is told plainly, with no explanation given.

think: When someone in power shows mercy to a defeated enemy, how would you tell whether it is generosity, self-interest, or a mistake?
